opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it comes down to aligning incentives. Pharma and biotech partners have watched a lot of computational promises come and go. Plenty of platforms showed a nice benchmark, then the molecules fell apart once they hit the wet lab. So the first thing that matters is that we're not just selling software and walking away. We're working on the problems our partners actually care about, against the targets they've struggled with, and we're accountable for whether the output is useful.

The second piece is that the models have gotten good enough to change the economics of early discovery. If you can design binders or antibodies with a much higher hit rate, maybe you test tens of designs instead of screening huge libraries. That compresses timelines and cuts costs in a way partners can feel right away. And it opens up targets that were considered undruggable or too expensive to go after. That's not a marginal efficiency gain. It changes which programs are even worth starting.

Third, partners get the benefit of a team whose whole job is pushing the frontier of these models. Most pharma companies are great at biology, chemistry and clinical development, but building and constantly improving frontier generative models is a different muscle. Partnering lets them plug into that without rebuilding it internally, and they get the improvements as the models get better.

Finally, structuring deals around shared success, with milestones and downstream value instead of only fees, signals that we believe in what we're producing. That kind of skin in the game builds trust. Partners know we only win when the molecules actually work. In drug discovery, that's ultimately the only thing that matters.

r001.rationale: The response says Chai’s deals are structured around shared success and that “we only win when the molecules actually work,” tying the company’s success to partner outcomes.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the simplest way to put it is that we're not asking partners to bet on a tool, we're asking them to bet on an outcome. A lot of the AI-for-drug-discovery space historically has been software licensing: here's a platform, here's a model, pay us a seat fee and go figure out how to make it useful inside your own org. And the problem with that is the model is only one piece. You still need the wet lab, the assay development, the iteration loop, and the people who actually know how to read what the model is telling them.

What we do instead is take on a real portion of the risk. We work with a partner on a specific target, we design the molecules, we run the validation, and the economics are structured around whether we actually deliver a binder or a candidate that hits the profile they care about. So the incentives are aligned in a way they just aren't with a pure software deal. If we don't produce something, we don't get paid in a meaningful way. If we do, we share in the upside, which could be milestones and royalties down the line.

The other thing I'd point to is speed. With Chai-2, we're getting to validated hits on a lot of targets in a single round, where traditionally you'd be looking at months of screening and multiple cycles. For a pharma partner, that compresses the part of the pipeline that's usually the most unpredictable. So you're not just getting a molecule, you're getting a much tighter distribution on how long it takes to get there, and that changes how they plan programs.

And then honestly, the last piece is that it's a way for them to access frontier modeling capability without having to build it themselves. Building a lab that can do both the ML and the experimental work at this level is really hard, and most companies would rather partner for it than spend years trying to replicate it internally. So it's less "buy our software" and more "let's co-develop this and both win if it works," and I think that framing is what makes people lean in.

r001.rationale: The response says Chai takes on risk and is paid meaningfully only if it delivers a molecule meeting the partner’s goals, with shared upside if successful. This communicates that Chai’s success depends on partner success.

astra-6.text: I think the appeal is that we can help partners get to a useful molecule faster and with less experimental work. They bring the biological problem and the expertise to develop a drug, and we bring the ability to design molecules against that problem. If that works, the value is much bigger than simply making one step in their workflow cheaper. You’re potentially making a program feasible that otherwise wouldn’t have been. And that creates an opportunity to structure partnerships around shared success.

r001.rationale: The response mentions structuring partnerships around “shared success,” but does not clearly state that Chai Discovery’s success as a company depends on its partners’ success.

sol-6.1.text: I think the appeal is that we can align the business model with the outcome the partner actually cares about. They don’t want to buy a model just to have a model; they want a molecule that solves a particular problem. If we can help them get there faster and with less experimental work, that’s a very tangible source of value. And a partnership lets us participate in that value while they bring the biological expertise and development capabilities needed to turn a promising molecule into a medicine.
